questions.q: Two point masses of 2.0 kg are each 0.50 m from an axis of rotation. What is their total moment of inertia about the axis?
questions.solution: For point masses, \(I = \Sigma mr^{2}\). Each mass contributes \(2.0 \times 0.50^{2} = 0.50\ \text{kg m}^{2}\), so the total for both is \(1.0\ \text{kg m}^{2}\). Forgetting to square the distance gives twice this.

questions.q: A flywheel has a moment of inertia of \(2.0\ \text{kg m}^{2}\) and rotates at \(10\ \text{rad s}^{-1}\). What is its rotational kinetic energy?
questions.solution: \(E_{k} = \frac{1}{2}I\omega^{2} = \frac{1}{2} \times 2.0 \times 10^{2}\) = 100 J. Forgetting the half (200 J) or forgetting to square the angular speed (10 J) are the usual slips.

questions.q: Two flywheels have the same mass and radius and spin at the same angular speed. One is a solid disc; the other has most of its mass in a heavy rim. Which stores more energy, and why?

options.A: The rimmed flywheel, because its mass is further from the axis, giving a larger moment of inertia.
options.B: The solid disc, because its mass is spread evenly.
options.C: They store the same energy, because they have the same mass.
options.D: The solid disc, because it has a larger moment of inertia.

questions.solution: Moment of inertia depends on how far the mass is from the axis: \(I = \Sigma mr^{2}\). Putting mass in the rim makes it larger. Since \(E_{k} = \frac{1}{2}I\omega^{2}\), the rimmed flywheel stores more energy at the same angular speed.

questions.q: A wheel speeds up uniformly from rest to \(30\ \text{rad s}^{-1}\) in 6.0 s. What is its angular acceleration?
questions.solution: \(\alpha = \frac{\Delta\omega}{\Delta t} = \frac{30}{6.0} = 5.0\ \text{rad s}^{-2}\). Multiplying instead of dividing (180) is the usual slip.

questions.q: A wheel starts from rest with a uniform angular acceleration of \(2.0\ \text{rad s}^{-2}\). Through what angle does it turn in 4.0 s?
questions.solution: \(\theta = \omega_{1}t + \frac{1}{2}\alpha t^{2}\), starting from rest: \(\theta = \frac{1}{2} \times 2.0 \times 4.0^{2}\) = 16 rad. The value 8.0 is the final angular speed, not the angle.

questions.q: A wheel of moment of inertia \(3.0\ \text{kg m}^{2}\) has an angular acceleration of \(4.0\ \text{rad s}^{-2}\). What resultant torque acts on it?
questions.solution: \(T = I\alpha\) = 3.0 × 4.0 = 12 N m. This is the rotational form of Newton's second law, with torque in place of force and moment of inertia in place of mass.

questions.q: A spinning skater has a moment of inertia of \(6.0\ \text{kg m}^{2}\) and an angular speed of \(3.0\ \text{rad s}^{-1}\). She pulls in her arms, reducing her moment of inertia to \(2.0\ \text{kg m}^{2}\). What is her new angular speed?
questions.solution: With no external torque, angular momentum is conserved: \(I_{1}\omega_{1} = I_{2}\omega_{2}\). So \(\omega_{2} = \frac{6.0 \times 3.0}{2.0} = 9.0\ \text{rad s}^{-1}\).

questions.q: A motor delivers a torque of 50 N m while rotating at \(20\ \text{rad s}^{-1}\). What is its output power?
questions.solution: \(P = T\omega\) = 50 × 20 = 1000 W. This is the rotational form of power equals force times velocity.

questions.q: A gas is compressed: 300 J of work is done on it, and during the compression it loses 100 J of energy by heating. What is the change in its internal energy?
questions.solution: First law: \(Q = \Delta U + W\), where \(Q\) is energy supplied by heating and \(W\) is work done by the gas. Here Q is −100 J and W is −300 J, because work is done on the gas. So the internal energy rises by 300 − 100, an increase of 200 J.

questions.q: An ideal gas expands isothermally. What does the first law of thermodynamics say about this change?

options.A: The energy supplied by heating equals the work done by the gas.
options.B: No energy is supplied by heating.
options.C: No work is done by the gas.
options.D: The internal energy of the gas increases.

questions.solution: Isothermal means constant temperature, and the internal energy of an ideal gas depends only on its temperature. So the change in internal energy is zero, and all the energy supplied by heating is used to do work: \(Q = W\).

questions.q: A gas is compressed adiabatically. What happens to its temperature, and why?

options.A: It stays the same, because no energy is transferred by heating.
options.B: It falls, because the gas does work.
options.C: It falls, because energy leaves the gas by heating.
options.D: It rises, because the work done on the gas increases its internal energy.

questions.solution: Adiabatic means no energy is transferred by heating. Work is done on the gas as it is compressed, and with nowhere else to go this energy raises the internal energy, so the temperature rises. This is how the air in a diesel engine gets hot enough to ignite the fuel.

questions.q: What does the area enclosed by the loop on a pressure–volume diagram for an engine cycle represent?

options.A: The energy supplied by burning the fuel.
options.B: The net work done in one cycle.

questions.solution: The area under each curve on a pressure–volume diagram is the work done in that process. Around a closed loop, the work done by the gas minus the work done on it is the area enclosed: the net work done per cycle.

questions.q: The indicator diagram for one cylinder of an engine has an area of 400 J. The engine has 4 cylinders, each completing 20 cycles per second. What is the indicated power?
questions.solution: Indicated power = area of loop × cycles per second × number of cylinders = 400 × 20 × 4 = 32 000 W, which is 32 kW. Leaving out the number of cylinders (8.0 kW) is the usual slip.

questions.q: A heat engine operates between a hot source at 600 K and a cold sink at 300 K. What is its maximum theoretical efficiency?
questions.solution: Maximum efficiency = \(\frac{T_{H} - T_{C}}{T_{H}} = \frac{600 - 300}{600}\) = 0.50. The temperatures must be in kelvin, and no real engine reaches this limit.

questions.q: What does the second law of thermodynamics imply for any heat engine?

options.A: It must reject some energy to a cold sink, so it can never be completely efficient.
options.B: It can convert all the energy from its source into work if friction is removed.
options.C: It works best when the source and sink are at the same temperature.
options.D: It creates energy as it runs.

questions.solution: A heat engine needs both a hot source and a cold sink, and some of the energy taken from the source must be passed to the sink. So even an ideal engine with no friction cannot turn all the energy it takes in into work.

questions.q: A heat pump uses 1.0 kW of electrical power to extract 3.0 kW from the air outside a house. What is its coefficient of performance as a heat pump?
questions.solution: The power delivered to the house is the work input plus the power extracted: 1.0 + 3.0 = 4.0 kW. Coefficient of performance of a heat pump = \(\frac{Q_{H}}{W}\) = 4.0 ÷ 1.0 = 4.0. The value 3.0 would be its coefficient as a refrigerator.
